description.en: A hypothetical EU reference architecture for regional LiveKit SFU clustering, NATS signaling, and separate WebRTC and HLS audience paths.

content.en:
When a WebRTC system grows past one media node, the hard problems stop being about video codecs and start being about seams.

Signaling has one view of the room. Media routing has another. Redis or NATS carries partial state. a separate HLS delivery path serves a different audience shape. If those seams are not designed deliberately, the platform still works in demos but becomes expensive and unpredictable under real load.

This is a hypothetical multi-region EU reference architecture. The HonarAmoozesh implementation it draws from used LiveKit, NATS, and WebRTC for live sessions; its HLS playback was available hours later and was not a current-session audience path.

The architecture is not just “add more SFUs.” It is deciding which state is global, which media should stay regional, and when a viewer should leave the real-time path entirely.

## The failure mode I optimize for

Most real-time media platforms do not fail all at once.

They degrade in specific places:

- a room lands on a hot SFU while another node is underused
- signaling promotes a user before media routing is ready
- a student on a weak network forces aggressive bitrate adaptation
- cross-region participants create unexpected egress paths
- a webinar audience behaves like a broadcast, not a meeting

The important design distinction is between interactive users and passive viewers. Teachers, moderators, and active students need low-latency WebRTC. Most spectators do not. Keeping everyone on the same real-time path makes the system more expensive without improving the learning experience.

That is where a clustered SFU plus a separate HLS delivery path becomes useful.

## Regional SFU topology

For an EU deployment, I would start with regional SFU pools rather than one large central media cluster.

A practical first topology:

- Frankfurt as the primary central EU region
- Strasbourg or Paris as a secondary nearby region
- Amsterdam as an optional north-west expansion point
- room placement based on teacher location, expected audience, and compliance constraints
- capacity tracked per SFU node, not only per Kubernetes pod

The goal is not to route every packet through the geographically nearest server. The goal is to keep the room stable. If a teacher is in Frankfurt and most active participants are in Germany, pinning the room to Frankfurt is often better than moving participants dynamically between regions.

Dynamic routing sounds elegant, but unstable routing can create worse user experience than a slightly longer RTT. For live education, predictable behavior matters more than theoretical optimality.

## State coordination: Redis or NATS is not optional glue

A clustered SFU needs a shared view of room state.

At minimum, the system has to answer:

- which node owns this room?
- which participants are connected?
- which tracks are available?
- which node is under pressure?
- which sessions can be moved safely?

Redis can work as the fast coordination layer for room presence and participant-to-node mapping. NATS is useful when the system needs explicit event flow: role changes, room lifecycle events, recording triggers, and moderation actions.

In the LiveKit + NATS pattern, I prefer to keep signaling events explicit. A teacher becoming a speaker, a moderator muting a participant, or a student moving from viewer to active participant should be represented as an event with a clear owner. That keeps the media plane simpler and makes debugging possible when a live class is under pressure.

## WebRTC for interaction, HLS for scale

The biggest cost mistake is treating every user like an interactive participant.

For education platforms, the audience is mixed:

- teachers need real-time publishing
- moderators need real-time control
- selected students need interactive audio/video
- most students often need reliable viewing

WebRTC is excellent for the first three groups. HLS is better for large passive audiences because it reduces pressure on SFU egress and handles unstable client networks more gracefully.

The hybrid design is straightforward:

- keep active participants on LiveKit WebRTC
- push a clean mixed or selected stream into HLS for passive viewers
- promote viewers into WebRTC only when they need to interact
- make promotion an explicit state transition, not a frontend trick

This is where NATS-style signaling helps. A role promotion is not just a UI change. It changes media routing, permission checks, and capacity planning.

## Cost reduction through audience-path separation

Cost reduction in this pattern does not come from one magic optimization.

In this hypothetical reference design, cost would be reduced by stacking several boring decisions:

- fewer passive viewers on expensive real-time paths
- regional SFU placement to reduce unnecessary egress
- adaptive bitrate and simulcast to avoid over-sending video
- a separate HLS delivery path for broadcast-shaped traffic
- clear room ownership so sessions do not bounce between nodes
- measuring cost per live minute instead of only CPU or bandwidth

The important metric is not “how many users can one node handle.”

The better metric is:

- cost per live classroom minute
- p95 join time
- p95 media reconnect time
- SFU egress per room
- percentage of users on WebRTC vs HLS
- number of role promotions per session

Those numbers tell you whether the architecture is serving the product, not just whether the infrastructure is busy.

## What I would monitor from day one

For a clustered LiveKit deployment, I would not wait for scale to add observability.

The first dashboards should include:

- per-node participant count
- per-node outbound bitrate
- packet loss by region
- ICE failure rate
- reconnect rate
- room placement decisions
- WebRTC to HLS ratio
- role promotion latency
- NATS or Redis event lag

The most useful alert is not “CPU is high.”

A better alert is: “Frankfurt rooms with more than 300 passive viewers are still sending too many users through WebRTC.” That points directly to product and routing behavior.

## What still needs care

A regional SFU design introduces its own risks.

Cross-region rooms can become expensive if tracks are forwarded carelessly. Redis state can become a hidden dependency if failover is not tested. a separate HLS delivery path can hide real-time quality problems if the team only watches aggregate availability.

A future implementation would need deliberate failure testing:

- kill one SFU during an active class
- delay NATS events and watch role promotion behavior
- simulate a regional packet-loss spike
- force a separate HLS delivery path during a high-attendance session
- test whether moderators can recover the room without engineering help

This is the difference between a media demo and an operable platform.

## The engineering lesson

LiveKit SFU clustering is not only a scaling technique. It is a product decision about who really needs real-time media.

For EU-scale live education, I would design the system around three paths:

- WebRTC for active interaction
- HLS for passive scale
- explicit signaling events for role and routing changes

That combination keeps latency low where it matters, reduces egress where interaction is not needed, and gives operators a model they can reason about during incidents.

The core lesson is simple: real-time media fails at the seams between signaling, routing, and fallback paths. If those seams are explicit, the platform can scale. If they are implicit, every growth milestone becomes an incident waiting to happen.
